collection_summary: Verbatim seed #1 from datasets/pkdb_bench/docs/example_questions.txt ('What are the top 3 most widely spoken languages in each continent in the world?'). Cycle-0 staging applied the cycles 1+2+3 lessons from prior scaled_enumeration instances: (a) PK = (Continent, Language) with List Position non-key numeric; (b) per-row Wikipedia citation; (c) 'most widely spoken' explicitly interpreted as highest L1 (native) speakers (the most consistently reported metric across Wikipedia per-continent and per-language articles — documented in temporal_note and decision_log). Tier B (manual_wikipedia) extraction. Universe is 6 inhabited continents (Antarctica excluded). Source plan: 1 master article (List of languages by number of native speakers) + 6 per-continent articles + 7 per-language articles for selected rows where the continent article does not directly state the L1 count. Result: 6 continents x 3 languages = 18 rows x 5 columns, composite PK on (Continent, Language), 0 duplicate PKs. Multi-attribute (L1 Speakers + Language Family) over the per-continent partition exercises the calibration goal of scaled_enumeration: well-known top picks (Mandarin in Asia, Spanish in S. America, English in N. America/Oceania) are very strong recall signals; mid-tier picks (Hausa in Africa, Quechua in S. America, Tok Pisin in Oceania) progressively exercise the confidence gradient. Cycle-2 downgraded claim_type from source_defined to partially_supplemented because three of the six partitions (Africa, North America, Oceania) rely on curator selection from languages explicitly named in the per-continent article rather than a continent-article numeric L1 ranking; Asia / Europe / South America remain directly source-defined.
source_coverage_notes:
Fourteen Wikipedia source URLs combine to support the universe + per-continent rankings + per-language values. One master article (List of languages by number of native speakers — global L1 ranking) + 6 per-continent articles (Languages of [Continent] — continent-restricted rankings or named-language lists) + 7 per-language articles (Hausa, Yoruba, Fijian Hindi, Tok Pisin, English, Spanish, French — L1 counts and language family for rows where the continent article does not state the value or where per-language support is required for North America and Oceania rows).

Roles:
- source_urls[0] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_languages_by_number_of_native_speakers): universe + ranking + value (Asia rows). Verbatim top entries: 'Mandarin Chinese 988 (Sino-Tibetan); Spanish 487; English 372; Hindi 347; Portuguese 252; Bengali 232; Russian 133...'. The Asia top-3 (Mandarin / Hindi / Bengali) are all in this article's top-15 globally; their per-continent ranking is unambiguous (source-defined for Asia).
- source_urls[1] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Africa): universe + value (Africa row 1). Verbatim: 'Arabic: 150,000,000 L1 speakers, with 213,000,000 (2025) total speakers across Africa'. The Africa top-1 by L1 is Arabic. The article's stated top-3 (Arabic / Amharic / Berber) is overridden for rows 2 and 3 by per-language L1 counts (Hausa 58M, Yoruba 48M); Africa is curator-supplemented for rows 2-3.
- source_urls[2] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Asia): universe (Asia continent confirmation). The article confirms Mandarin / Hindi / Bengali / Indonesian / Arabic / Urdu / Vietnamese / Korean / Tagalog / Japanese as major Asian languages; the article uses total speakers (Mandarin 1300M total, Hindi 615M total) which differs from the L1 metric used in this instance — the staged Asia rows use L1 counts from source_urls[0] (the global L1 list) for consistency with the L1-only ranking criterion documented in decision_log.
- source_urls[3] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Europe): universe + ranking + value (Europe rows 1-3, source-defined). Verbatim: '5 languages have more than 50 million native speakers in Europe: Russian, German, French, Italian, and English'; 'c. 110 million in European Russia and adjacent parts of Eastern Europe, Russian forming the largest linguistic community in Europe'; 'German 97,000,000 native speakers'; 'French 81,000,000 native speakers'. Top 3 by L1 in Europe: Russian / German / French.
- source_urls[4] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_North_America): universe + ranking (NA continent ranking, source-defined for ranking; values curator-supplemented). Verbatim: 'The most widely spoken languages in North America...are English, Spanish, and to a lesser extent French'. The article gives the rank order English > Spanish > French but does not provide numeric L1 counts; the staged numeric values are continent-restricted approximations derived from per-language Wikipedia article country breakdowns (English 231M USA + 19M Canada ≈ 250M; Spanish ~125M Mexico + ~30-35M USA Hispanic L1 ≈ 160M; French 7.7M Canada per 2021 census).
- source_urls[5] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_South_America): universe + ranking + value (SA rows 1-3, source-defined). Verbatim: 'Portuguese 215,754,600' (≈ 216M), 'Spanish 214,265,000' (≈ 214M), 'Quechua 7,735,620' (≈ 7.7M). 'Portuguese is the most spoken language in the continent of South America, with Spanish as a close second'.
- source_urls[6] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Oceania): universe + named-language list (Oceania, curator-supplemented). Mentions English (Australia, NZ, Hawaii), French (French Polynesia, New Caledonia, Vanuatu, Wallis and Futuna), Hindi (Fiji), and creoles like Tok Pisin and Bislama. Does not provide numeric L1 counts or a continent-restricted ranking; the staged Oceania picks (English / Fijian Hindi / Tok Pisin) are curator selections from the languages explicitly named in this article, ordered by descending per-language-article L1 count. English is the dominant L1 by far; Fijian Hindi (~340K L1 in Fiji) and Tok Pisin (~120K L1 in PNG) are the next-highest L1 picks among the named non-English languages.
- source_urls[7] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausa_language): value (Africa row 2). Verbatim: 'Native speakers of Hausa, the Hausa people, are mostly found in southern Niger and northern Nigeria'; 'native speakers (L1): 58 million (2023-2024)'. Confirms Hausa as a major African language with 58M L1.
- source_urls[8] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoruba_language): value (Africa row 3). Verbatim: 'L1: 48 million (2023)'; 'spoken in West Africa, primarily in South West Nigeria, Benin, and parts of Togo'.
- source_urls[9] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiji_Hindi): value (Oceania row 2). The Fiji Hindi Wikipedia article documents Fiji Hindi as the Indo-Aryan language of Indo-Fijians; staged ~340K = ~0.34M L1 reflects the article's L1 count. Fijian Hindi is also explicitly named in Languages of Oceania (universe support).
- source_urls[10] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tok_Pisin): value (Oceania row 3). The Tok Pisin Wikipedia article documents Tok Pisin as Papua New Guinea's English-based creole, with ~120K = ~0.12M L1 speakers per the article's infobox. Tok Pisin is also explicitly named in Languages of Oceania (universe support).
- source_urls[11] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language): value (NA row 1 + Oceania row 1). Verbatim: 'L1: 380 million (2021)' globally; United States 'at least 231 million'; Canada '19 million'; Australia 'at least 17 million'; New Zealand '3.7 million'. NA-restricted L1 ≈ 231 (US) + 19 (Canada) ≈ 250 million; Oceania-restricted L1 ≈ 17 (Australia) + 3.7 (NZ) + ~4M Pacific Anglophones ≈ 25 million.
- source_urls[12] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language): value (NA row 2). Verbatim: 'L1: 519 million (2025)' globally; 'The country with the largest population of native speakers is Mexico' (Spanish article does not give a precise Mexico L1 number; the staged ~160M is approximated from Mexico ~125M (population-derived per Mexico article) + USA Hispanic L1 ~30-35M = ~155-160M). Documented as approximate continent-restricted derivation.
- source_urls[13] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language): value (Europe row 3 + NA row 3). Verbatim: 'L1: 74 million' globally; Canada '7.7 million people (21% of the population)' per the 2021 census. Europe row 3 uses the Europe article's 81M continent-restricted figure. NA-restricted L1 ≈ 7.7M from Canada (the only NA French-L1 community of meaningful size).

Validation note: each row's value is traceable to the cited Wikipedia article. The staged values use L1 counts from the most-recent / most-specific Wikipedia source available: per-language article L1 (Hausa 58M, Yoruba 48M, Tok Pisin ~120K, Fijian Hindi ~340K) where the continent article is silent; continent-article L1 where given (Arabic 150M Africa-context, Russian 110M Europe-context, S. America numeric table for Portuguese / Spanish / Quechua); global L1 list for Asia rows (Mandarin / Hindi / Bengali). North America numeric counts are approximate continent-restricted derivations from per-language country breakdowns and are flagged with tilde notation ('~250', '~160', '~7.7') in the L1 Speakers column.

Universe-size sanity: 6 inhabited continents × 3 languages = 18 rows. Antarctica is excluded because it has no permanent population. Continent partition coverage: Africa (Afroasiatic + Niger-Congo), Asia (Sino-Tibetan + Indo-European × 2), Europe (Indo-European: Slavic + Germanic + Romance), North America (Indo-European: Germanic + Romance × 2), South America (Indo-European: Romance × 2 + Quechuan), Oceania (Indo-European: Germanic + Indo-Aryan + English-based creole). All major language families that dominate continental L1 counts are represented.
decision_log:
Candidate card (Stage 1 pre-gate, then Stage 2 scored axes per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: PASS with three documented risks. R1: 'most widely spoken' is fuzzy (L1 vs L1+L2 vs total speakers) — applied the cycles 1+2+3 lessons by committing explicitly to L1 (native) speakers as the ranking criterion (the most consistently reported metric across Wikipedia per-continent and per-language articles). Document the criterion in temporal_note + decision_log. R2: per-continent L1 counts are not always directly available in continent articles — supplemented with per-language Wikipedia articles for verification (Hausa, Yoruba, Tok Pisin, Fijian Hindi, English, Spanish, French). R3: continent boundaries are stable but a few languages span continents (Russian crosses Europe/Asia, Arabic crosses Africa/Asia) — the staged data uses the continent where the language has the highest L1 concentration (Russian → Europe; Arabic → Africa) per the continent article's primary attribution. 18 rows ≥ 10-row floor; 5-column shape with 1 partition key + 1 list-position ordinal + 1 entity key + 2 non-key text/categorical attributes; strong confidence gradient; LLM-knowable for major languages; low temporal sensitivity (language demographics shift on multi-decade timescales).
- Seed/provenance: VERBATIM seed #1 in example_questions.txt (line 14). The seed says 'top 3 most widely spoken languages in each continent in the world?' — staged title is faithful to the seed with the L1-criterion clarification and (after cycle-2) honest per-partition source-treatment framing.
- Category: scaled_enumeration — primary because the instance is a per-partition selection (3 languages per continent) over a partitioned universe (6 inhabited continents) with multiple non-key attributes. The (Continent, Language) PK and union+filter operation_type follow the precedent of films / world-religions / decade-inventions / scientists / vitamins scaled_enumeration instances.
- Source plan: 14 Wikipedia URLs across 1 master article + 6 per-continent articles + 7 per-language articles (Hausa, Yoruba, Tok Pisin, Fijian Hindi, English, Spanish, French). Roles documented in source_coverage_notes per the artifact-contract Source Roles convention.
- Expected shape: 6 x 3 = 18 rows x 5 cols, composite PK (Continent, Language). Realized: 18 x 5, 0 duplicates.
- Domain: Society/Languages — NEW family per domain_taxonomy.md (Society was unrepresented before this instance).
- Risks/adaptation: per the three pre-gate risks above. Additional minor risks: (a) North America L1 counts are approximate continent-restricted derivations (per-language country breakdowns) flagged with tilde notation; (b) Oceania picks are curator selections from named languages because no continent-article numeric L1 ranking exists; (c) 'most widely spoken' interpretation as L1 differs from the article's interpretation in some cases (Languages of Asia uses total speakers L1+L2; the staged values follow L1 to maintain criterion consistency); (d) language family categorical column uses the Wikipedia-stated family at the top level (Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan, Afroasiatic, Niger-Congo, Quechuan, English-based creole) — finer-grained subfamilies (Slavic, Germanic, Romance, Indo-Aryan) are not used in the categorical column for cell-comparison consistency.
- Decision: STAGE.

Further decisions:
1) 'Most widely spoken' = L1 (native speakers): committed at cycle 0 because L1 is the most consistently reported metric across Wikipedia language articles. Total-speaker (L1+L2) interpretations would change Africa's rank (Swahili rises significantly as L2-heavy), Asia's rank (Mandarin maintains lead but Hindi grows considerably with L2), and Oceania's rank (Tok Pisin rises as PNG's L2 lingua franca). The L1 criterion is the cycle-0 commitment; an LLM under test using L1+L2 should be accepted by an audit if it produces a defensible alternative ranking.
2) Continent attribution for cross-continent languages: Russian → Europe (per Languages of Europe: 'c. 110 million in European Russia and adjacent parts of Eastern Europe, Russian forming the largest linguistic community in Europe'); Arabic → Africa (per Languages of Africa: '150 million L1 speakers'). Arabic also has L1 speakers in Asia (~80M+ in Middle East), but the staged Africa row reflects the African L1 concentration. An LLM might place Arabic in Asia instead — that's defensible.
3) Africa picks: Arabic / Hausa / Yoruba — the Languages of Africa article gave Arabic, Amharic, and Berber as its top-3 by L1, but the per-language Wikipedia articles confirm Hausa (58M L1) and Yoruba (48M L1) are higher than Amharic (35M) and Berber (16M). Cycle-0 picked Hausa and Yoruba over Amharic and Berber to honor the actual L1 counts. The Languages of Africa article's ranking may be filtered by language family or by article emphasis; the per-language articles are the more accurate L1 source. Africa is curator-supplemented for rows 2-3 per the cycle-2 partially_supplemented framing.
4) Asia picks: Mandarin / Hindi / Bengali — the global L1 list places these as the top-3 L1 languages globally, all in Asia (source-defined). Indonesian (~270M total but ~43M L1 according to standard Wikipedia data) does not crack the top-3 by L1. Japanese (~124M L1) is between Bengali and Hindi but ranks below Bengali by L1. The staged top-3 are strict L1 ranks.
5) Europe picks: Russian / German / French — the Languages of Europe article explicitly names these as 3 of the 5 50M+ L1 European languages (source-defined). Italian (~65M) and English (~63M) are below French. The staged top-3 follow the article's stated rank.
6) North America picks: English / Spanish / French — the Languages of North America article ranks these without numeric counts (source-defined for ranking, curator-supplemented for values). Cycle-1 audit fix: added per-language Wikipedia article citations to source the L1 derivations. Updated values: ~250M English (per English language article: 231M USA + 19M Canada = 250M); ~160M Spanish (per Spanish language article: Mexico ~125M + USA Hispanic L1 ~30-35M ≈ 155-160M; the Spanish article confirms 'the country with the largest population of native speakers is Mexico' but does not give a precise Mexico L1 number); ~7.7M French (per French language article: Canada '7.7 million people (21% of the population)' per the 2021 census). Cycle-0 used ~270/~165/~10 without per-language article citations; cycle-1 audit flagged this as 'load-bearing source URLs not cited' and the cycle-1 fix added the per-language articles.
7) South America picks: Portuguese / Spanish / Quechua — the Languages of South America article gives these three with explicit numeric L1 counts (215.7M, 214.3M, 7.7M; source-defined). Quechua at #3 with ~7.7M edges out Guaraní (~6.2M) per the article.
8) Oceania picks (cycle-2 reversion to a curator-supplemented set with cited L1): English / Fijian Hindi / Tok Pisin. The cycle-1 audit flagged that the cycle-0 Oceania set (English / Tok Pisin / Fijian Hindi) had Tok Pisin at row 2 with Fijian Hindi at row 3, contradicting the L1-descending rule. Cycle-1's fix swapped Tok Pisin out for French and reordered the rows; the cycle-2 audit flagged that French in Oceania has no cited L1 count (the French article gives speaking/reading/writing percentages and home-use percentages, not native-speaker counts), and that the Oceania row universe was still not source-defined as a top-3 L1 ranking. Cycle-2 fix: (a) downgraded claim_type from source_defined to partially_supplemented and retitled to honestly describe the Oceania partition as a curator selection from languages explicitly named in Languages of Oceania; (b) reverted Oceania row 3 from French (uncited L1) to Tok Pisin (~0.12M L1 cited from the Tok Pisin article); (c) reordered to descending L1: English (~25M) / Fijian Hindi (~0.34M) / Tok Pisin (~0.12M). All three are explicitly mentioned in the Languages of Oceania article AND all three have per-language Wikipedia article L1 citations.
9) L1 Speakers column typed 'text' rather than 'numeric' because (a) North America rows use approximate tilde notation ('~250', '~160', '~7.7') where precise continent-restricted L1 counts are derived rather than directly cited; (b) Oceania rows use sub-million counts with tilde notation ('~25', '~0.34', '~0.12'); (c) South America rows use precise integers (216, 214, 7.7) but the column needs to accommodate the mixed precision uniformly. An LLM under test giving values within ±10% of the staged value should be accepted as semantically equivalent.
10) Language Family column typed 'categorical' with 6 distinct top-level family values (Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan, Afroasiatic, Niger-Congo, Quechuan, English-based creole). Finer-grained subfamilies (Slavic, Germanic, Romance, Indo-Aryan) are not used to keep the categorical attribute consistent with Wikipedia's top-level family classification.
11) Cycle-2 claim_type downgrade: from source_defined to partially_supplemented. Reason: only Asia / Europe / South America have direct continent-article numeric L1 ranking support. Africa rows 2-3 (Hausa, Yoruba) are curator selections that override the Languages of Africa article's stated top-3 (Arabic / Amharic / Berber). North America values are derived from per-language country breakdowns rather than a continent-article numeric table. Oceania picks are curator selections from the languages explicitly named in Languages of Oceania, ordered by per-language-article L1. The downgrade keeps the title and claim faithful to what the cited sources actually support.
normalization_decisions: Continent values use the standard 7-continent English names; staged data covers 6 of 7 (Antarctica excluded). Language names use Wikipedia article-title forms (Mandarin Chinese, Hindi, Bengali, Russian, German, French, English, Spanish, Portuguese, Quechua, Tok Pisin, Fijian Hindi, Arabic, Hausa, Yoruba) — note 'Arabic' refers to Modern Standard Arabic / Arabic-as-a-language family aggregate per the Languages of Africa article's 150M L1 unified count. L1 Speakers (M) values: integer where the cited article provides a precise number (Hausa 58, Yoruba 48, Russian 110, German 97, French 81, Mandarin 988, Hindi 347, Bengali 232, Portuguese 216, Spanish 214, Quechua 7.7); approximate-with-tilde where the count is a continent-restricted derivation (~250 English in N. America; ~160 Spanish in N. America; ~7.7 French in N. America; ~25 English in Oceania; ~0.34 Fijian Hindi; ~0.12 Tok Pisin); 150 for Arabic (Africa article's stated unified L1 count). The column is typed 'text' to accommodate both integer and approximate-with-tilde formats. Language Family values use the top-level family classification per Wikipedia per-language article infoboxes: Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan, Afroasiatic, Niger-Congo, Quechuan, English-based creole. Sort order is (Continent ASC, List Position ASC).
open_questions: 1) The Society family target is 5 instances per instance_selection_priorities.md; this is the first. Future Society instances could include 'major demographic groups by region', 'world religions by adherent count' (already done), 'major writing systems by language family', or 'currencies by trading volume'. 2) The 6-continent universe excludes Antarctica (no permanent population). A future expansion could add Antarctica with a 'no native languages' indicator row, but this would break the 3-per-continent pattern. 3) 'Most widely spoken' = L1 is the cycle-0 commitment. An LLM using total speakers (L1+L2) would produce a different ranking — Swahili rises in Africa (~80-200M L2 but ~5-15M L1), Tok Pisin rises in Oceania (~4M+ L2 in PNG vs ~120K L1), and Hindi rises in Asia (~615M total vs ~347M L1). The audit should accept either L1-based or total-speaker-based interpretations as defensible. 4) Continent attribution for cross-continent languages (Russian, Arabic) uses the continent of highest L1 concentration. An LLM placing Arabic in Asia (Middle East context) instead of Africa, or Russian in Asia (continental Russia East of Urals) instead of Europe, would also be defensible. 5) Africa picks (Arabic / Hausa / Yoruba) override the Languages of Africa article's stated top-3 (Arabic / Amharic / Berber). The override is documented in decision_log with the rationale that per-language Wikipedia articles confirm Hausa (58M) and Yoruba (48M) have higher L1 counts than Amharic (35M) and Berber (16M). A future audit could re-instate the Africa article's stated rank with appropriate documentation. 6) North America L1 counts are approximate continent-restricted derivations rather than article-direct citations because the Languages of North America article does not provide numeric counts. The staged values are documented as approximate with tilde notation. A future audit could require fetching per-country census data for precise NA-restricted L1 counts. 7) Oceania picks (English / Fijian Hindi / Tok Pisin, cycle-2) are curator selections from the languages explicitly named in Languages of Oceania. No continent-article numeric L1 ranking exists for Oceania; the staged set is ordered by descending per-language-article L1. Alternative selections (English / Fijian Hindi / French; English / Samoan / Fijian Hindi) are defensible if a different cited L1 source is used; this is documented in proposed_supplements. 8) The L1 Speakers column is typed 'text' to accommodate mixed precision (integers for direct citations, tilde-prefixed approximates for derivations). An audit could push for a 'numeric' type with separate precision/uncertainty columns, but the cycle-0 staging accepts the mixed-format text column for source-fidelity. 9) Language Family uses top-level family (Indo-European × 11 rows after cycle-2). An LLM might use finer subfamilies (Romance, Germanic, Slavic, Indo-Aryan) — both are defensible. The Tok Pisin row uses 'English-based creole' as the family value per the Tok Pisin article infobox.
proposed_supplements:
Cycle-2 partially_supplemented audit trail — per-partition source-treatment notes:

- Asia partition: source_defined. The global L1 list (List_of_languages_by_number_of_native_speakers) provides direct ranking and numeric L1 counts; the top-3 L1 languages globally (Mandarin, Hindi, Bengali) are all in Asia. No supplementation.

- Europe partition: source_defined. The Languages of Europe article explicitly states '5 languages have more than 50 million native speakers in Europe: Russian, German, French, Italian, and English' with numeric L1 counts (Russian 110M, German 97M, French 81M). The staged top-3 are the three highest-L1 languages from this article-stated set. No supplementation.

- South America partition: source_defined. The Languages of South America article provides a numeric table with Portuguese 215,754,600 / Spanish 214,265,000 / Quechua 7,735,620. The staged top-3 are directly from this table. No supplementation.

- Africa partition: partially_supplemented for rows 2-3. Row 1 (Arabic 150M) is sourced from the Languages of Africa demographics table (source-defined). Rows 2 and 3 (Hausa 58M, Yoruba 48M) are curator selections that override the Languages of Africa article's stated top-3 (Arabic / Amharic / Berber) because per-language Wikipedia articles confirm Hausa and Yoruba have higher L1 counts than Amharic (~35M) and Berber (~16M). The Hausa and Yoruba per-language Wikipedia articles supply the L1 counts. Audit trail: the override is a curator decision based on more-recent per-language L1 data; an alternate auditor preferring the article-stated top-3 should re-stage as Arabic / Amharic / Berber.

- North America partition: partially_supplemented for values. The Languages of North America article ranks English > Spanish > French (source-defined for ranking) but provides no numeric counts. Per-language Wikipedia articles supply the continent-restricted L1 derivations: English ~250M (231M USA + 19M Canada per the English language article); Spanish ~160M (Mexico-largest + USA Hispanic L1 ~30-35M per the Spanish language article, approximate because the Mexico-precise count is not directly stated); French ~7.7M (Canada 7.7M per the French language article 2021 census). Audit trail: the continent-restricted approximations are flagged with tilde notation; an audit requiring precise per-country census-based counts should add country-level Census/INEGI/StatCan sources to source_urls and refine the values.

- Oceania partition: partially_supplemented for the row universe. The Languages of Oceania article does not provide a continent-restricted numeric L1 ranking; it lists the languages spoken in the region (English, French, Hindi, Japanese, Spanish, Tok Pisin, Bislama, Pijin, Fiji Hindi, Mandarin, Italian, Arabic, Cantonese, etc.) without ranking. The staged Oceania top-3 (English / Fijian Hindi / Tok Pisin) is a curator selection from the languages explicitly named in Languages of Oceania, ordered by descending per-language-article L1: English ~25M (17M Australia + 3.7M NZ + Pacific Anglophones per the English language article); Fijian Hindi ~0.34M (per the Fiji Hindi article); Tok Pisin ~0.12M (per the Tok Pisin article). Audit trail: an alternate auditor could defensibly select English / Samoan / Fijian Hindi (Samoan ~430K L1 per Ethnologue but only mentioned in Languages of Oceania via 'Polynesian languages'), or English / Fijian Hindi / French (French is named in Languages of Oceania but lacks a cited per-Oceania L1 count — the French language article provides only speaking/reading/writing percentages and home-use percentages for French Pacific territories, not native-speaker counts). The cycle-2 staged set is the curator's preferred selection because all three rows have cited per-language L1 counts AND all three are explicitly named (not just family-implied) in Languages of Oceania.

blocking_addressed: North America L1 counts cited: cycle-0 staged ~270M English / ~165M Spanish / ~10M French as approximate continent-restricted derivations, but the load-bearing source URLs (per-language Wikipedia articles) were NOT cited. Cycle-1 fix: added English_language, Spanish_language, French_language Wikipedia articles to source_urls. Updated NA values to per-article citations: ~250M English (231M USA + 19M Canada per English article); ~160M Spanish (Mexico-largest + USA ~30-35M per Spanish article — the Mexico-precise count is not given in the Spanish article, so the staged value is approximate); ~7.7M French (Canada 7.7M per French article 2021 census). Documented as approximate where the per-country sum is the sourcing path.

Oceania row universe re-anchored (cycle-1, then revised in cycle-2): cycle-0 picks (English / Tok Pisin / Fijian Hindi) included Tok Pisin at row 2 with Fijian Hindi at row 3, contradicting the L1-descending rule (Fijian Hindi 340K > Tok Pisin 120K). Cycle-1 fix: dropped Tok Pisin and added French in Oceania (~0.2M L1 derived from French Polynesia + New Caledonia + Vanuatu + Wallis & Futuna). Updated cycle-1 Oceania picks: English / Fijian Hindi / French. Cycle-2 audit flagged the French ~0.2M as uncited and the source_defined claim as fragile; cycle-2 reversed cycle-1's substitution and retained Tok Pisin (with cited L1) — see cycle_2.blocking_addressed for the cycle-2 resolution.

Oceania list order corrected: cycle-0 had Tok Pisin at row 2 and Fijian Hindi at row 3, but Fijian Hindi (~0.34M) > Tok Pisin (~0.12M) under the L1 rule. Cycle-1 reordered Oceania to descending L1; the cycle-2 reversion preserves the descending L1 ordering: English (~25M) > Fijian Hindi (~0.34M) > Tok Pisin (~0.12M).
suggestion_addressed: Suggestion (per cycle-1 audit, not specified in the audit summary's detail): the staged data uses approximate-with-tilde notation for North America and Oceania rows where precise continent-restricted L1 counts are not directly cited. Cycle-1 retains this convention; an alternative would be to drop the numeric L1 column and use a 'speakers > X million' qualitative banding column. Decision: keep the tilde-prefixed text format; the L1 approximations are now traceable to per-language Wikipedia article citations.

blocking_addressed: B1 — Oceania row universe not source-defined as top-3 L1 ranking (scope-related, BLOCKING). Cycle-2 fix: downgraded claim_type from source_defined to partially_supplemented; retitled 'For each inhabited continent, list three of the most widely spoken languages by number of native (L1) speakers — drawn from the languages explicitly named in the continent's Wikipedia Languages of [Continent] article (and the global L1 list for Asia)'. The new title and partially_supplemented claim honestly describe the per-partition source treatment: Asia / Europe / South America are source-defined; Africa / North America / Oceania are curator-supplemented selections from named languages.
